#5346. South Korea Delays Its Crypto Tax to 2029, a Fourth Postponement That Still Needs Lawmakers’ Approval

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

South Korea’s government will push its 22% crypto tax back two years to 2029, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said on Thursday, November 5, a day after Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok asked for the delay.

Korean traders have now heard “not yet” four times.

The levy would charge 22%, a 20% national rate plus 2% local tax, on yearly gains from virtual assets above ₩2.5 million, about $1,860. It was due to start in January 2027. Lee announced the plan at an emergency briefing at the Government Complex Seoul, saying the ministry will consult with the National Assembly on a two-year deferral.

It is a quick turn. As recently as the summer, the government had confirmed the tax would go ahead in January 2027, with no new delay in its yearly tax plan.

So why does Seoul keep moving the date, and did Korea’s crypto market even notice?

The official reason this time is data. Tax information exchange with the US on crypto accounts starts in 2029, and the ministry says taxing earlier would leave users of local exchanges worse off than traders on offshore platforms the tax office can’t yet see.

Lee gave three reasons in all. Besides the US exchange, he named the need to refine the rules, including deductions for carried-over losses, and the trading and regulatory changes coming with Korea’s digital asset act.

The loss rule matters most for traders. Under the current law, gains and losses are counted one year at a time. The government now wants losses carried forward for up to three years and deducted from later gains, pointing to how far crypto prices swing.

Politics did the rest. Seoul Economic Daily wrote that the deciding factor was fading support among young adults, who make up most of Korea’s crypto investors, and both the ruling and opposition parties had called for another delay.

Lee said he takes it “seriously” that he is announcing another deferral after three earlier ones.

The tax was written into law in 2020 and first set for January 2022. Lawmakers moved it to 2023 in December 2021, to 2025 in December 2022, and to 2027 in December 2024.

The new plan has its own schedule. A public-private working group will join international talks on sharing crypto tax data, rule changes come in the first half of 2027, amendments go to the National Assembly’s regular session that year, and detailed tax standards follow in the first half of 2028.

One caveat: none of this is law yet. The statute still says January 2027 until lawmakers pass an amendment, though the request came from the ruling party’s own leader.

For now, very little changes. Gains stay untaxed for two more years if the amendment passes, and the market barely moved on the news.

Upbit’s KRW markets traded ₩1.36 trillion, about $1.01 billion, in the 24 hours to 14:33 UTC on Thursday. XRP led with ₩146.7 billion, or 10.8% of the total, ahead of Bitcoin’s ₩114.3 billion.

Korean prices are almost level with global ones. Bitcoin cost ₩107.05 million on Upbit, about $79,570 at ₩1,345 per dollar, just 0.1% above Binance. That gap, the “kimchi premium”, tends to widen when local demand runs hot.

XRP, Upbit’s most traded coin, sits at $1.30 on Binance, down 14% in 30 days. It trades below the 50-day EMA at $1.3348 and the 200-day EMA at $1.3628, with resistance at $1.3444 and support at $1.2562. Below that, the next swing low is $1.2002.

Korea’s traders get another two years without a bill. Whether 2029 sticks depends on the same lawmakers who moved the date three times before.

#5345. Tether CEO Reacts to Massive USDT Demand in Paraguay

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino has responded to claims that the company's stablecoin, USDT, is being increasingly sought after in Paraguay following a significant banking crisis that cut off millions of people from their savings. Ardinoino has described this as "a flight to safety."

As noted in a recent X post by Bitcoin proponent Samson Mow, Tether's USDT has seen a significant rise in value relative to the Paraguayan guaraní amid the collapse of Ueno Bank, one of Paraguay's biggest digital lenders.

Ueno Bank, with an estimated 3 million customers (a significant percentage of adult Paraguayans), has been hit by a major financial crisis.

According to Mow, USDT has risen from 5,692 guaraníes to over 6,000 guaraníes, an increase of over 5%.

The surge in interest in the U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin USDT, Mow argues, is due to people trying to safeguard their savings outside of the traditional banking system.

USDT's exchange rate rose from about 5,692 guaraníes on Oct. 15 to over 6,000 on Nov. 4.

It is worth noting that even the traditional U.S. dollar rose against the guaraní over the same period.

The rising interest in USDT comes as Paraguay faces a major financial crisis over the collapse of Ueno Bank.

On Nov. 3, Paraguay's central bank announced the start of resolution proceedings for the financial institution after discovering that Ueno Bank's solvency ratio had dropped below half the minimum limit.

The move essentially shut down Ueno Bank, cutting off millions of customers' access to their savings and standard banking services for the time being.

The crisis has also cast doubt on public funds parked at Ueno Bank, including hundreds of millions of dollars from Paraguay's social security system.

The scandal has reportedly already led to the arrest of eight people connected to the bank as well as the resignation of central bank president Carlos Carvallo, as reported by Reuters.

Paraguay's central bank has been trying to reassure depositors, stressing that the situation pertains specifically to Ueno Bank and is not indicative of the collapse of the country's banking system.

Customers with frozen funds at Ueno Bank cannot necessarily convert their deposits to stablecoins until they are able to access their money again.

#5344. Food delivery startup Wonder files for IPO as it explores its next big bite

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.

Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.

Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

#5343. Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense

Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.

The funding comes almost one year to the day after the Los Angeles-based company announced a $160 million Series C, which included an initial truck order from FedEx. Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

The Series D was co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s “technology impact fund,” and defense-focused firm Ridgeline. FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen. Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)

While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen. The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors. FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.

Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis. The company has steadily expanded its efforts since. It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI, has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles, and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.

According to a fresh investigation by Santiment, retail investors, giving in to "fear of missing out" on Hyperliquid (HYPE) price rally on October 30, gave four large wallets a perfect opportunity to fully close their positions, bagging $5 million in profit.

Wall Street legend Stan Druckenmiller's first ever appearance on X (former Twitter) with a post about Hyperliquid and the tokenization of trading was supposed to be a declaration of a new era for the popular DeFi exchange. It turned out to be a "sell the news" signal for HYPE tokens' whales.

The best example of 'cashing out' math was educated by the address "0xa2ce...3126". What was a constant accumulation since the end of May, at the peak of the pump, in the $94–$95 range for HYPE token, became a methodical dump worth exactly $225,000 on the market every five minutes. All this was happening while the crowd bought up on the news. The result is a completely empty wallet and its owner locking in $2,395,168 gains.

This whale was not alone in his approach and as Santiment stresses, citing its own on-chain data, four top players opened short positions simultaneously and are now in profit. The only big buyer who believed in HYPE price growth is losing more than 11%.

The token's price chart against USD only confirms a total exodus of big buyers at the time of writing. The Oct. 30 pump candle left a huge upper wick with a trace of those very five-minute sales. The HYPE price has already slid more than 12% and is squeezed in the $81.79–$85 range. The local level of $84.150 has been broken from top to bottom, and now the token is slowly drifting to the next strong support at $78.020.

Traditional finance's 'big guns' like Druckenmiller undoubtedly remain the best marketing tool for crypto projects. The only difference is that for retail investors a billionaire’s tweet became a call to action, and for big capital an exit order.

The buyers’ rush created a perfect liquidity window for the whales — a chance to sell off huge volumes of coins without the price slipping down. What this makes of the story is that the technology and business of Hyperliquid turned out not to equal the price of decentralized exchange's native token.

Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR), the Nasdaq-listed company holding 38.9 million HYPE, has applied to the CFTC to become a futures commission merchant, it said Thursday, a license that would let it carry US client accounts on Hyperliquid’s tokenized stocks markets.

🇺🇸 JUST IN: Hyperliquid Strategies, holding $3.5 BILLION in $HYPE, officially files to become a US futures broker.The Nasdaq-listed firm says a subsidiary has applied to become a futures commission merchant, a broker regulated by the CFTC.If approved, US customers could trade… pic.twitter.com/nZE00MELkS

Over the 24 hours to 09:56 UTC on Friday, stocks, indexes and oil on trade.xyz, Hyperliquid’s biggest builder market, traded $9.75 billion. Hyperliquid’s own crypto perpetuals did $9.69 billion. Two days earlier, the stock side was at $4.99 billion.

Its quarterly report, out the same day, showed $13.3 million in revenue for the three months to September 30, above analyst estimates of $10.6 million to $12 million, and $620.6 million in net income, almost all of it paper gains on HYPE.

Markets did not cheer. PURR closed at $8.76 on Thursday, down 9.6% on the day, and HYPE fell 6.9% to $77.75 by Friday morning.

So what would the license change, and why did tokenized stocks on Hyperliquid just out-trade crypto?

Hold American traders’ accounts and money for Hyperliquid markets. A futures commission merchant is the broker in US futures: it takes customer deposits and margin and places orders on regulated exchanges.

The accounts would be for HIP-3 markets, the upgrade that lets outside teams launch their own markets on Hyperliquid. “Independent operators would run their own market in a compliant manner, while the chain underneath would stay a neutral infrastructure layer,” the company said in its release.

CEO David Schamis tied it to the HYPE bet. “Setting up an FCM is how we intend to help bring markets deployed on Hyperliquid onshore,” Schamis said.

It fills the last gap in a plan that has moved fast. On October 29, NYSE owner ICE agreed to run an exchange and clearing house for markets designed by TradeXYZ, the team behind trade.xyz. An FCM would give US traders an account to reach them.

There is a catch. “There can be no assurance as to the timing or outcome of the application or regulatory approval of permissioned HIP-3 markets,” the firm said. And a group backed by Cboe and Citadel Securities sued the CFTC on November 3 to stop US stock perps altogether.

By $60 million over the last day. Trade.xyz lists 143 markets, and its $9.75 billion edged past the $9.69 billion traded across Hyperliquid’s 235 crypto perpetuals, with $4.43 billion in open interest on the stock side.

These are perpetual futures that track a share price. Traders get price exposure around the clock with leverage, but no share changes hands.

The chip selloff did the rest. Six chip and memory markets in trade.xyz’s top 10 traded $3.59 billion between them, 37% of the total:

The XYZ100 tech index led everything at $1.31 billion, ahead of the S&P 500 at $1.0 billion. Both fell 4%.

Almost all of it from staking. HYPE staking and validator commissions brought in $12.3 million, and interest on cash added $1.0 million.

The $620.6 million profit came from the token. It booked $803 million in unrealized gains on HYPE, less a $172.3 million tax provision.

That mark has already slipped. The company held 38.52 million HYPE on September 30, worth $3.51 billion at $90.99. At Friday’s $77.75, the same tokens are worth about $510 million less.

PURR has lost 29% since closing at $12.29 on October 29, the day of the ICE deal. At $8.76, it sits below the $10.36 average price at which it has sold shares.

HYPE trades at $77.75, down 6.9% in 24 hours and 15.2% in a week. It has given back the whole ICE rally, which peaked at $97.74 on Binance on October 29, and sits 20.6% under its $97.96 record from September 23.

RWA Foundation's report, based on Token Terminal data, now signals an infrastructure-scale gap in the volume of institutional funds between Stellar and XRP Ledger, two blockchain techs that share the same origin thanks to Jed McCaleb. Stellar became for Franklin Templeton the second network in terms of significance after BNB Chain, surpassing even Ethereum.

Almost all RWA liquidity inside Stellar is shared between four of the biggest platforms. The undisputed leader remains Spiko, holding about half of the market there with $2 billion in tokenized funds. Second comes Franklin with its flagship fund, while the BlackRock-backed Ondo and Realiz split the remainder, commanding about half a billion dollars each.

«Franklin Templeton decided to add another hundred million just as we were about to publish…», researchers noted in comments to the report release.

The most striking demonstration of the gap between Stellar and XRPL is in the stablecoin segment. Amid similar numbers in how many of them are on both of the chains, 'digital dollars' on the XLM-linked chain are more used in commercial payments where their monthly transit volume hit $20.48 billion. On XRPL the same metric is at $9 million, which proves that they are simply held on balance without real usage in the ecosystem's payment tunnels.

The spike in Stellar dynamics in the second half of 2026 is backed by successful integrations inside the industry. Chainlink's price oracle has been locked in, while a key long-term factor is guaranteed by a joint venture with the US central repository DTCC which is expected to be the direct release of traditional financial vehicles into on-chain space by the first half of 2027.

#5338. AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months

Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.

This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.

Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.

Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum.

#5336. After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

#5335. Bitcoin Opens to Russian Savers With a 300,000-Ruble Cap, Just 0.048 BTC a Year Per Broker: How Much Can Russians Really Buy?

Russians without qualified-investor status will be able to buy Bitcoin, Ether and Tether’s USDT through brokers, but only up to 300,000 rubles a year each, under Bank of Russia rules officially published on Friday, November 6.

At Friday’s prices, that is about $3,668, or 0.048 BTC.

The cap was set out in Directive No. 7441-U, signed by Governor Elvira Nabiullina on September 11 and registered with the Justice Ministry on October 30. It takes effect 10 days after publication, on November 17. Qualified investors face no limit.

The venue is almost ready. The Moscow Exchange plans to open trading in BTC, ETH and USDT on December 1, starting with pilot trades. Sberbank and VTB are among 25 companies on the central bank’s register of licensed crypto exchangers as of Friday.

The cap has lost value since it was proposed. By a Tokenist calculation, 300,000 rubles bought 0.057 BTC on August 11 and 15% less now.

So how much Bitcoin can a Russian saver actually buy, and what changes on December 1?

About 0.048 BTC a year through each broker. We converted the cap at the Bank of Russia’s official dollar rate, 81.79 rubles on Friday, and Binance’s BTCUSDT price.

The amount has moved with both the ruble and BTC:

Selling does not free up room. The directive counts the cap as the ruble sum of what a non-qualified investor paid for crypto through a broker during the calendar year, so a buyer who sells in March cannot use that money to buy again until January.

Every investor must also pass a test first. The Bank of Russia said in August that all buyers, qualified or not, need to pass it and read the risks before trading, and that the cap applies separately at each intermediary, whether broker, crypto exchanger or asset manager.

Why only three coins? The law limits retail buyers to assets with large market value and trading volume, and at least five years of price history on foreign venues.

One caveat: the directive itself only covers purchases through brokers, so how the limit works at exchangers will depend on their own rules.

Discover: Bitcoin Sits on Its 200-Day Average as Democrats Close In on Both Chambers of Congress: Is the Crypto Market Structure Bill Out of Time?

Russia gets an organized crypto market. The Moscow Exchange said on November 2 that it plans to let market participants trade digital currencies from December 1.

The start will be slow. “In the first stage, pilot trades are expected, with participants connecting to the new market gradually as they become ready,” the exchange said.

Banks are lining up to sell crypto directly too. The central bank’s register of crypto exchangers lists 25 companies as of Friday, including Sberbank, VTB and T-Invest Lab. Sberbank has said it plans to launch its first crypto products on December 1.

The rules also close older doors. The Bank of Russia says individuals cannot send crypto to non-custodial wallets. From July 1, 2027, residents will be able to trade only through licensed intermediaries.

Discover: Bitcoin Sellers Take a Week of Losses Below $80,000 as Strategy and Strive Keep Buying: Will $75,000 Hold?

BTC trades at $75,772, down 0.4% on the day, after Thursday’s sell-off took it below its 200-day exponential moving average (EMA) for the first time since August.

Russian retail money will arrive in small amounts at first. For Bitcoin, the 200-day EMA matters more this month than the cap.

#5334. XRP Ledger Welcomes New Euro Stablecoin

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) community has welcomed a new stablecoin to the blockchain. This time, it's via GateHub, which is launching a new euro-pegged stablecoin for blockchain payments that links the blockchain to the traditional European banking network.

As announced in a press release on Nov. 5, GateHub partnered with Slovenian financial services company Dinaro to launch GateHub Euro (EURGH), a MiCA-compliant (European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation) stablecoin pegged to the euro.

The new stablecoin operates on both the XRP Ledger and Xahau, an alternative blockchain in the larger XRPL ecosystem with smart contract capabilities.

Part of the significance of EURGH is its SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) integration. With this, GateHub users can make instant euro payments from their XRPL and Xahau wallets to banks in Europe.

GateHub notes that these transactions can take just seconds to complete, linking blockchain assets to the traditional banking world.

GateHub Euro is a stablecoin that is designed to maintain a value of exactly one euro. This means 1 EURGH should equal €1. It is an electronic money token (EMT) under the EU's MiCA regulations.

GateHub Euro is issued by Dinaro, which is an authorized electronic money institution regulated by the Bank of Slovenia.

According to Dinaro's published terms, it will issue EURGH on a 1:1 basis when it receives Euro funds. Holders of the token will be able to redeem EURGH for Euros at face value (subject to proper checks and compliance procedures).

GateHub users can access traditional European payment systems via their digital wallets because of the SEPA integration. This is an alternative to traditional crypto exchanges for converting funds into the traditional banking network.

GateHub Euro is not the first euro-pegged stablecoin to emerge in the crypto space or on the XRP Ledger.

For instance, there's the MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin EURØP from Schuman Financial.

Meanwhile, there's Circle's EURC, which is a euro-pegged stablecoin for payments and trading on multiple blockchains.

And there's EUR CoinVertible (EURCV) from Société Générale-FORGE, a digital asset business unit of French banking giant Société Générale.

Ripple CEO Bradley Garlinghouse is pushing back against the idea that the company’s growing RLUSD stablecoin ambitions come at XRP’s expense, insisting the stablecoin is targeting a different market altogether.

By targeting the wider market, Ripple hopes to expand the range of financial applications operating on its blockchain. Garlinghouse emphasized that the company wants RLUSD-powered use cases to run on XRPL, potentially attracting more businesses, developers, and institutional users to the network.

Garlinghouse was responding to XRP community researcher WrathofKahneman, who argued that RLUSD’s expansion could ultimately benefit XRP by increasing liquidity across the XRP Ledger. “RLUSD is great for XRP. #5331. Your iPhone Duo Under Attack? Binance Flags Dangerous iOS Security Flaw

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance has warned Apple users about a dangerous iOS vulnerability that could expose crypto wallets, private keys, and login credentials. The flaw, called worse_query, allows malicious applications to access files normally isolated inside other apps. Binance warning identifies several affected iOS software versions and urges users to remove untrusted applications immediately.

The vulnerability threatens more than crypto wallets; apps storing sensitive information locally could also expose passwords, authentication data, and personal files. That makes the latest warning particularly concerning for iPhone users who rely on their devices for banking and crypto transactions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

Binance says the problem affects iOS itself rather than its own wallet infrastructure. Users who suspect their devices have been compromised should create new wallets on clean devices and move their funds. The exchange also recommends resetting active login sessions and updating installed software.

The vulnerability exploits Apple’s application sandbox, a security mechanism designed to keep applications separated from one another. Normally, an application cannot freely access another application’s private files. This isolation protects sensitive information even when users install multiple applications on the same device.

This is where it gets dangerous: the worse_query exploit reportedly bypasses those restrictions. A malicious application could potentially access directories containing information belonging to other installed applications.

The researcher behind the public GitHub repository describes worse_query as a sandbox escape affecting iOS 26 and iOS 27. The project identifies affected releases spanning iOS 26.0 through 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2. Binance warns that exposed information could include cryptocurrency recovery phrases, private keys, and login credentials.

The actual danger depends partly on how individual applications store sensitive information. Wallets retaining recovery phrases or other credentials in accessible local files face particular risks.

Security researchers have also highlighted the importance of protecting plaintext wallet information. SlowMist’s security chief warned that the vulnerability could undermine assumptions about isolation between application containers.

Apple’s security update schedule adds another dimension to the Binance iOS warning. Apple’s security releases list iOS 27.2 and iOS 26.7.2 among its available software versions, both released on October 26, 2026.

However, Apple’s published security advisories do not explicitly identify worse_query by name. There is currently no confirmed public statement establishing that these updates fully resolve the specific sandbox escape.

A separate GitHub project implementing the exploit also reported on November 8 that Apple’s available software releases had not patched worse_query. This leaves users with an important gap between installing the latest available update and confirming that a particular vulnerability has been fixed.

Binance recommends installing the latest official iOS release and keeping all applications updated. It also urges users to remove applications from unknown sources, including manually signed IPA files.

For us, crypto holders, the safest response to suspected compromise goes beyond simply deleting suspicious software.

The latest iPhone warning follows several security incidents involving malicious applications and crypto credentials. In September, Binance warned users about FomoPeek, a third-party application whose versions 1.1 and 1.2 reportedly contained malicious code.

Security researchers found that the software could exploit iOS vulnerabilities to obtain elevated device privileges. Potentially exposed information included recovery phrases, private keys, login credentials, and other locally stored data.

More recently, CertiK highlighted the DarkSword exploit framework, which reportedly targeted cryptocurrency applications through compromised websites and vulnerable iPhones.

#CertiKInsight 🚨 A new version of DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit, is being used to target crypto wallets on unpatched iPhones. Simply opening a malicious site in Safari can be enough: no wallet connection, no signature needed. Here's what you need to know 🧵

These incidents involve separate attack methods. Nevertheless, they demonstrate why smartphone security has become increasingly important for crypto holders.

The Binance iOS warning highlights a fundamental problem with self-custody: protecting a recovery phrase means protecting every place where that information might be stored.

#5330. Crypto Industry Faces New Threat as Warren Eyes Powerful Senate Role

The cryptocurrency industry may face major regulatory hurdles following the Democrats' victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

Longtime cryptocurrency critic Elizabeth Warren is set to lead one of the Senate's most powerful committees, according to a Nov. 5 report by The Wall Street Journal.

The WSJ report by Corrie Driebusch and Dylan Tokar described Warren's 20-year record of clashing with Wall Street, holding bankers accountable, delving into private equity and examining big financial firms.

Chairing the Senate Banking Committee would also give Warren more power to conduct investigations and issue subpoenas.

The news means greater oversight in Congress and potentially more scrutiny of the cryptocurrency industry, a sector that has often clashed with Warren over financial regulation. It could lead to even more hurdles for industry-friendly laws.

Warren is among the most vocal critics of the cryptocurrency sector in Washington.

Back in March 2023, her reelection campaign famously endorsed her "anti-crypto army" campaign, something cryptocurrency proponents took great offense to.

Warren has often tied cryptocurrency to money laundering, ransomware, sanctions busting, and other financial crimes.

Recently, Warren has opposed Republicans' push for the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. She says the bill lacks sufficient consumer protections and financial crime safeguards.

In a Sept. 15 Senate speech, she argued that the U.S. should regulate crypto but opposed crypto bills designed to benefit the industry.

Should Warren take over the Banking Committee in January 2027, she will have much more say in which crypto proposals move forward and which industry executives are grilled.

Traditionally, a cooler-than-expected Consumer Price Index print is bullish for risk assets. Sentiment leans toward a soft-to-in-line outcome that would confirm inflation is decelerating after two firmer months, though markets remain sensitive to any upside surprise in core services or shelter components.

#5328. XRP Ledger's Biggest Lending Upgrade Just Got Closer

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) is on the verge of a significant decentralized finance (DeFi) upgrade that could potentially open up new lending possibilities and liquidity for the XRP Ledger network.

According to Vet (@Vet_X0), a notable XRPL validator and community member, the much-anticipated Lending Protocol amendment has now gained two more Yes votes from validators, moving one step closer to activation.

The Lending Protocol amendment now boasts 21 Yes votes from a total of 35 trusted validators (60%). The amendment needs eight more Yes votes to reach the minimum threshold of 29 validators.

Reaching this threshold doesn’t mean that the upgrade will instantly go live. Instead, reaching the supermajority threshold will initiate the mandatory two-week activation period, which requires a minimum of 80% of validators to support the amendment.

The upgrade, known as XLS-66, is geared towards adding a native lending feature to the XRP Ledger.

In contrast to most crypto lending services, where borrowers are typically required to provide more collateral than the loan amount, XLS-66 is specially crafted to enable fixed-term and non-collateralized lending.

This will enable qualified borrowers to secure loans without the need to hold cryptocurrency collateral that exceeds the loan amount.

According to the official XLS-66 document, the Lending Protocol will enable the pooling of funds via so-called Single Asset Vaults, which can then be loaned to borrowers under set terms.

The proposed lending system involves three key actors: depositors, loan brokers and borrowers.

While depositors are in charge of depositing crypto or supported assets into a vault, loan brokers are tasked with brokering lending deals as well as evaluating borrowers.

For their part, borrowers would receive the loans and pay them back based on the set schedule.

The upgrade could potentially empower financial institutions and other entities to put capital to use on the XRP Ledger, as opposed to just holding or moving around assets.

It may also open up new prospects for earning interest on deposited assets in lending vaults. The amount of interest, however, would largely depend on the actual lending activity and risks.

According to the latest validator data, this amendment has reached 23 out of 35 votes. It still requires six more votes to hit the threshold.

Furthermore, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment, which offers upgrades including closed-ended vaults, updated interest accounting, etc., also currently has 21 Yes votes.

All three amendments are currently being considered, and none has yet reached supermajority.

Oil has gone the other way. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell 17% from $117.64 on October 30 to $97.35 this morning, as traders bet on a deal to end the war with Iran.

That bet may be early. Amos Hochstein was an energy adviser to President Joe Biden. He told CNBC that the risk of renewed war is “still alive.” If fighting resumes, he said, gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel prices would all surge.

So if oil spikes again, does BTC fall further?

The drop came fast. Brent lost 10.9% on Monday, November 2, and another 8.7% on Wednesday, as traders bet that the fighting would end.

No deal has been signed. Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it had disabled a tanker that ignored warnings after visiting an Iranian port, and attacks on tankers near Oman have continued since the U.S. election.

#5325. Crypto’s Next Two Years Should Be About Survival, Not Competition: Vitalik Buterin

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has warned crypto executives to switch focus to collective security and survival rather than competition between platforms. This follows multiple hacks that drained billions from the market and crushed traders’ sentiment.

In an interview with MoneyControl, Buterin urged crypto executives to focus on protecting user assets as a collective, as that could shape how regulators approach the sector. The next couple of years are key, as frameworks are still expected in several jurisdictions.

Digital asset firms, particularly centralized exchanges, have focused on gaining a larger share of the market cap, onboarding more users, etc but this buzz around gains leaves room for bad actors. For Buterin, the actions in the next couple of years will determine the long-term roadmap.

Most crypto users agreed with the Ethereum executive because, without asset safety, centralized exchanges will see capital exodus and more backing from traditional finance firms.

Recently, several crypto companies were hacked, including Binance, the largest centralized exchange by trading volume. Bad actors flagged in North Korea drained $6 billion; although large parts were recovered, it still remains the largest crypto hack of all time.

This week, Brazil’s largest exchange, Mercado, also suffered a breach that temporarily suspended trading. In a nutshell, these losses could prompt regulators to tighten requirements, setting the sector back.

Previously, regulators in the US and Europe often cited investor-protection concerns to delay major developments that would open the sector to traditional capital. Notably, spot crypto ETFs are a top example, although things changed after the White House backed the move following President Trump’s election win.

Buterin also added that recent attacks now target user interfaces and centralized components rather than smart contracts. He called for more operations to move on-chain, citing Binance Smart Chain and others.

“One good decision that Binance made is that they also launched Binance Smart Chain. They also benefit from the fact that if you do things with contracts on-chain, you can have very high levels of security. I am expecting we’re going to see more moves in that direction.”

On Ethereum security, Buterin and developers rolled out a roadmap to protect assets ahead of Q-Day. The network is lauded for taking early steps ahead of others as supercomputers get more powerful.

#5324. $7.6 Trillion in October: Broadridge’s Distributed Ledger Repo Platform Hits Processing Record

Broadridge Financial Solutions has shared data on the use of its Distributed Ledger Repo (DLR) platform to execute and settle repurchase agreement (repo) transactions. In October 2026, $7.6 trillion in repo transactions were executed using the platform. This represents an average daily volume of $345 billion.

Repo transactions involve the temporary sale of securities with an agreement to repurchase them at a specified price. In practice, repos are a form of short-term borrowing, with the securities serving as collateral. They’re commonly used by financial institutions to raise cash and manage their funding needs.

Broadridge’s DLR platform uses a distributed ledger to execute and settle repo transactions. The company has also recently unveiled a new platform called DLX that can be used to issue, trade, settle, custody, and service tokenized assets throughout their lifecycles.

Broadridge global head of digital innovation Horacio Barakat noted that earlier implementations of blockchain in financial services focused on individual use cases, but now, for tokenized assets to be adopted by banks, broker-dealers, and asset managers, it’s important to think about how they can be implemented within existing workflows and infrastructure. Barakat expects to see more institutions do this in 2027.

It’s worth noting that the $7.6 trillion in repo transactions executed in October is the total notional value of repo transactions during the month. Repo transactions are constantly churning, with new transactions being executed to replace expiring ones.

This data therefore gives a sense of the level of activity in the securities financing market using Broadridge’s DLR platform but doesn’t provide insights into crypto market activity or investor appetite for Bitcoin and Ether.

It also doesn’t provide insights into the amount of new capital flowing into crypto.

To understand the extent to which Broadridge’s DLR platform provides benefits around faster transfer of collateral and settlement, it would be helpful to have data around settlement times and the flow of collateral. Nevertheless, the data does give a sense of the level of securities financing activity using the platform.

#5322. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) has picked Avalanche as the only blockchain to settle tokenized stocks on its planned 24/7 trading platform, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of real companies. The NYSE version would let investors trade U.S. stocks around the clock, settle trades instantly and pay with stablecoins, digital tokens that hold a steady $1 value.

The New York Stock Exchange has selected Avalanche ($AVAX) as the exclusive blockchain for settling tokenized U.S. stocks on its upcoming 24/7 trading platform, according to the WSJ.NYSE cited Avalanche’s speed, throughput and compliance capabilities.The platform is targeting… pic.twitter.com/uE4S3X5lnn

AVAX jumped on the news. It rose 4.3% in the minute the reports hit at 12:30 UTC, and it trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% on the day while Bitcoin and Ether are down.

The pick lands on a chain that holds only a small slice of the market today. Avalanche carries $179 million of the $3.73 billion in tokenized shares tracked by rwa.xyz. That is 4.8% of the market, down from 10.3% a month ago.

So can the NYSE deal make Avalanche the main home for these tokens?

The plan is not new, but the blockchain is. NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) first announced the platform in January and said it would seek regulatory approval.

The tokens would not be copies. ICE said they would be interchangeable with ordinary shares and carry the same dividend and voting rights.

NYSE picked Avalanche for its speed, the number of trades it can handle, and its tools for meeting regulatory rules, the Journal reported. The platform is aiming for a fourth-quarter launch, but it still needs regulators’ approval.

ICE has also signed up Securitize to issue tokenized shares for companies and funds, under a deal announced this year.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The NYSE deal would be a big step up. We pulled the latest network breakdown from rwa.xyz, which tracks tokenized shares that investors can hold in their own wallets.

The market itself is still small next to the stock market. All the tokens it tracks add up to $3.73 billion, held by about 4.8 million wallet addresses.

The NYSE could change that scale. Every share settled through its platform would move on Avalanche, which no other chain can claim today.

There is a catch. Companies can refuse to have their shares tokenized. On OKXICE, a separate venue from OKX and ICE, 33 of the 62 companies first named had objected by late October.

Not yet. AVAX trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% from Monday’s opening price of $7.94, its best day since September 20.

The buying was heavy. In the hour that started at 12:00 UTC, about $11.8 million of AVAX changed hands on Binance. That is about 16 times a typical hour and the third-busiest hour in the past 1,000.

On the daily chart, AVAX is just below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs both sit at about $9.05, so one level now does the work of two.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

For tokenized stocks, the NYSE pick is the biggest vote yet for a single chain. For AVAX, the test is whether buyers can push it above $9.05 once the initial excitement fades.

The XRP Ledger continues to evolve with node memory usage reduced by up to 23% since the release of xrpld version 3.3.0. The release included several new amendments, as well as bug fixes and build improvements in August 2026.

RippleX developer Valentin Balaschenko shares a deep dive on how the memory consumption decline was achieved in an official blog post.

Memory growth in XRPL nodes was observed in late summer 2025. Operators reported increasing memory usage on their validators that did not decrease, including on nodes configured identically to others that were unaffected, and across different hardware platforms. The cause turned out not to be a memory leak but the memory allocator retaining memory the application had already freed, and a fix was shipped in xrpld 3.3.0.

A memory regression identified in one release during that period was addressed within weeks, but this had no observable impact for operators. The observed memory behavior existed before the regression and persisted after the fix. The underlying issue remained unresolved at the time. Operators monitoring node caches asked why memory did not come back after a cache sweep, the routine pass that clears expired entries.

Hussein Zangana (Vet), XRP Ledger Foundation director of community, mentioned this development in an X post: "Up to 23% memory savings on XRP Ledger nodes since 3.3.0. Given how expensive RAM is at the moment, this improvement is especially useful. Measured on (non/dUNL) validators as well as stock nodes, savings range from 13-23% depending on history."

The fixCleanup amendment was activated on the XRP Ledger this week on November 4, 2026, hardening and improving the XRP protocol.

The fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment is a collection of fixes for Single Asset Vaults, the Lending Protocol, Automated Market Makers, the permissioned DEX, trust lines, NFTs, MPTs, Escrow, Sponsorship, transaction signing, and permission delegation.

The fix upgrade changes VaultClawback to reject pseudo-account holders and updates VaultDeposit, VaultWithdraw, and VaultClawback to round more precisely, so vault assets can't over- or under-deliver. It changes VaultWithdraw to allow a fixed-share withdrawal to move zero assets from a fully impaired vault rather than failing. It also exempts an IOU issuer from their own global freeze on NFT offers in their own currency.

#5318. Adam Back Says Bitcoin Is Entering a Third Adoption Wave Led by Banks and Pension Funds

The CEO said Bitcoin is entering the third phase of global adoption, as interest from banks suggests BTC’s institutional demand is rising.

Bitcoin is about to enter its ‘third phase’ of global adoption, according to Adam Back, the CEO of Blockstream. In an interview this week (as tracked by Wu Blockchain), the legendary British cryptographer said BTC is preparing to enter this new growth phase. He termed it the ‘third phase’ of international adoption.

As per the CEO’s revelation, Bitcoin is entering a new phase of adoption. The executive indicated that the asset has had two stages of adoption. The first phase ran from 2011 to 2019. During this period, the decentralized currency attracted individuals to buy it and miners to mine it. During this time, BTC’s price surpassed $1 and later reached hundreds of dollars.

The second phase has been an institutional era from 2020 to the present. Institutional interest increased massively during this period, and BTC surged to a record $69,000 in November 2021, then climbed above $100,000 in August 2025. Institutional participation grew as ETFs validated Bitcoin’s legitimacy and made it easier for traditional investors to access.

In the podcast, Back said that the flagship cryptocurrency is on the verge of entering its ‘third wave’ of global adoption. According to the CEO, this period is unique and different from other phases. In this evolving era, traditional banks and other recognized investment institutions are preparing to further drive global Bitcoin adoption, the executive said.

As Back noted, the ‘third phase’ of institutional Bitcoin adoption is primed to be fueled by major investment banks and professional asset management channels, whose participation has yet to fully materialize.

The CEO revealed that some major investment banks have recommended a 2%-4% Bitcoin allocation in their model portfolios. Many mutual funds, pension funds, and insurance products now allow customers to gain indirect exposure to Bitcoin through their investment vehicles. In addition, Bitcoin treasury companies increasingly play this role.

Through this expanding third wave of adoption, Back believes that Bitcoin will be bought by the “world’s largest pools of capital.” He predicts that BTC will reach parity with Gold this cycle at a valuation of $1.5 million per coin.

#5317. Zcash (ZEC) OI Down 7.8% as NU7 Upgrade Goes Live

Zcash open interest has declined 7.8%, according to the data from analytical platform Coinglass.

Open interest (OI) refers to the value of futures contracts that are still open. In other words, the rise in OI means more active positions.

When a price and OI decline simultaneously, it usually suggests deleveraging. The traders might be closing positions or their positions might be liquidated.

ZEC is trading near $1,286, down 1.5% over the past 24 hours. The price’s pullback comes amid a broader market correction, with BTC down 5.75% in 24 hours.

Zcash gained 7.69% on November 4, rising on high expectations surrounding NU7. The upgrade introduces several changes to the network's transaction processing and reward structure.

As the upgrade went live on November 5, the target block interval went from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. According to the project’s statement, the change makes private payments confirm three times faster.

In addition to that, NU7 introduces a new transaction fee allocation model. 60% of the fees will go directly to a reserve for future network reserves, while the miners receive the remaining 40%.

Other changes include increased capacity for the Orchard shielded pool and new limits for wallet protection from spam.

So far, the market response has been mixed amid Friday’s correction. However, the ZEC chart is currently showing signs of an uptrend.

The price is testing support around $1,250, a level that could influence its next move. A sustained recovery above the $1,260-1,275 corridor would stabilize the further rebound.

On the other hand, a break below $1,230 would mean a failed recovery and a prolonged downtrend.

#5316. North Korea Hackers Launches Elon Musk Memecoins to Launder $6.4B Binance Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

North Korea backed hackers have created Elon Musk themed memecoins to launder stolen crypto in the $6.4 billion Binance hack. The hackers are using fake trading activity to disguise the movement of stolen funds.

One of the tokens featured Musk beneath an “Elon 2028 President” banner. Five others carried cartoon animals, crude jokes and familiar dog-coin branding. All six were created within three days and quickly abandoned.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic identified 117,000 NEAR tokens, worth $430,000, passing through the homemade coins between November 5 and November 7. The operation offers another look at how North Korea’s crypto laundering networks are adapting their techniques to move stolen assets.

Elliptic identified six newly created tokens on the NEAR blockchain: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI and SINU. Each token was paired with NEAR in its own decentralized exchange liquidity pool. The hackers then used one group of wallets to purchase the tokens with stolen NEAR before another group sold them back.

North Korea’s launderers are creating their own meme coins to move funds stolen from Binance.Between November 5 and 7, they launched at least six tokens on NEAR, dressed up with meme-coin logos such as a monkey in a pink bow and a duck in front of a US flag. Stolen NEAR went…

This separated the buying and selling wallets, preventing the stolen funds from moving directly between them. The transactions consequently resembled ordinary crypto trading, with the receiving wallets appearing to collect proceeds from successful memecoin trades.

Blockchain investigators could still follow the money. Elliptic found that almost all trading activity came from wallets connected to the laundering operation. Outside buyers accounted for less than 1% of one token’s trading volume.

The operation was also remarkably inexpensive. Creating each token cost just as low as 25 NEAR, or worth around $90. Five of the six token creators received funding from wallets that had already participated in earlier token sales.

The tokens were effectively disposable. All six stopped trading by November 8, with the creators of four withdrawing remaining liquidity.

The technique does not erase the transaction trail. Instead, it introduces additional steps that slow investigators trying to connect stolen funds with their eventual destinations. The firm previously identified a similar approach following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. North Korean launderers moved at least $24 million through homemade tokens using the same basic mechanism.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The memecoin operation represents only a small fraction of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance. The approximately $6.43 billion was taken from the exchange on October 29, making it the largest crypto theft ever recorded. Binance estimated its losses at $6.3 billion.

The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Investigators have identified multiple laundering techniques since the breach, including cryptocurrency swaps, cross-chain transfers, and movements through decentralized finance platforms.

Approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen, representing around 44% of the stolen assets. This leaves billions requiring further tracing as investigators race to identify wallets and freeze assets wherever possible.

The use of North Korean hackers and memecoins adds another disposable layer to this operation. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional exchanges or direct wallet transfers, hackers can manufacture trading activity around virtually worthless tokens.

Bitcoin Hyper is among the projects pursuing this approach, combining a Solana Virtual Machine-based execution environment with Bitcoin settlement. Its proposed infrastructure targets near-instant transaction finality alongside decentralized applications and DeFi functionality.

The project currently records more than $33.2 million raised in its presale, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136877 and staking rewards of 35% APY.

As crypto infrastructure continues to evolve, the race between increasingly sophisticated laundering networks and blockchain investigators is unlikely to slow down.

#5315. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5314. BSC Releases Reth Exploit Hotfix: Details About the Upgrade

BNB Smart Chain (BSC) has released a hotfix to its Reth execution client, BSC-Reth, according to the official announcement and a patch on Github. The patch addresses a vulnerability discovered on November 4, 2026, which could result in incorrect blockchain state-root calculations due to a bug in the legacy trie code (used to organize blockchain data).

Although the vulnerability could have resulted in financial loss, there is no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited or that funds were affected.

Rust Ethereum Harvester Tree, also known as Reth, is an execution client used to verify the data on the blockchain and process transactions. On November 4, 2026, a vulnerability was discovered in certain versions of Reth that could result in incorrect state-root calculations due to a bug in the legacy trie code.

This could potentially result in node disagreements and sync failures. The underlying bug was fixed in Reth pull request #28264, merged on November 3.

On November 6, BNB Chain published BSC-Reth v0.1.4-hotfix on GitHub. According to the release notes, this version includes a fix for incorrect state-root calculation in the legacy path in Reth. This version of BSC-Reth improves the way it deals with blockchain data, reducing the risk of incorrect state-root calculation during state verification.

All BSC-Reth node operators, including validators, MEV builders, full nodes, and sentry nodes, are advised to upgrade to this version and restart the node as soon as possible. This fix does not require a DB migration or hard fork. Users do not need to take any action. BNB Chain has also confirmed that this vulnerability has a limited effect on BSC-Reth and has no effect on opBNB.

The fallout triggers aggressive US government action: expanded export bans that effectively cut NVIDIA off from residual China-related revenue streams, congressional hearings that force Huang’s resignation, multiple shareholder lawsuits, and a broader regulatory cloud that freezes major data-center deals with hyperscalers wary of geopolitical risk.

Confidence in the company’s leadership and supply-chain integrity evaporates, competitors seize market share, and the AI spending boom that powered NVIDIA’s valuation begins to look overextended.

The most immediate and damaging development is the unfolding scandal itself. The 50-day and 200-day moving averages are rolling over, and momentum indicators such as RSI have spent time in oversold territory without producing a sustained bounce—often a sign that sellers remain in control.

A decisive break below the $180–$175 zone would open the door to a measured-move decline targeting the mid-$100s, with further downside possible if the $150 psychological level fails.
